summary.Summary: Nick Stene (as titled; introduced as Nick Steen), senior global insight manager for consumer health at Euromonitor, opened the Healthspan Summit on where the money in healthspan is going and which messages earn a premium [00:00] [00:20]. He said consumer health is growing about 5%, 1.5% without inflation, and this is the first year more is spent on prevention than on treatment [00:20]. OTC and sports protein both face profit pressure (tariffs and supply; premium whey costs), so money and $8 to $9 billion of deal finance are moving to premium dietary supplements [00:20]. Specific healthspan naming earns a premium while broad messaging is diluted, and ingredients lose their premium as they become popular, as magnesium forms have and NAD+ is starting to; postbiotics are his one to watch [00:20]. His takeaways: proof, knowing each ingredient's life stage, segmenting (especially perimenopause), and designing proof for shoppers, healthcare professionals and AI shopping agents [00:20].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Market: consumer health totals "373 billion" as he scopes it (currency not stated), growing about 5%, or 1.5 without inflation, half a point down; treatment has gone negative in real terms [00:20].
- Milestone: "the first year in which we have spent more physically on prevention than we have on treatment", and the gap between supplements and OTC will widen [00:20].
- OTC is hit hardest by tariffs, by dependence on active pharmaceutical ingredients from India and China, and, next, by European wastewater rules [00:20].
- Sports protein: he has shelf data showing a 20% plus pass-through in physical pricing, 30 to 40% overall once pack shrinkage and other absorption moves are counted; the premium whey supply problem "probably starts to get solved" around the back end of 2027, 2028 at the earliest, with "years of trauma" left [00:20].
- Money is moving to premium dietary supplements, through line extensions, brand actions and M&A; he sees "about eight to $9 billion in motion", some from venture capital and private equity outside health [00:20].
- Healthspan as a funnel: the edge (SKU names directly on age and life stage, including mitochondrial) is niche, growing and earns a premium; broader healthspan wording appears on cheap and expensive products alike; protection messages (immune, antioxidant) cover about half the shelf [00:20].
- Growth is stronger in shops than online, where trust is leaking; demographics explain about 30 to 40% of growth (people entering a new life stage, not the size of the ageing population), brand push about another third, and employers' attitudes to time off work more [00:20].
- On the US shelf, longevity and healthy ageing grow fastest and earn a strong premium; menopause is losing its premium while 40-plus and perimenopause still earn one; prostate has lost its premium; skin peaked in 2025 and hair is next; immune has peaked but remains a workhorse [00:20].
- Europe follows the same pattern, but mitochondrial messaging is already stronger than in the US, partly because of what the regulatory framework allows, and healthy-ageing messaging is "a tougher sell", some of it only online [00:20].
- Ingredient life cycle: proof brings a premium, popularity brings scale, then price war; magnesium forms "turned into footballs" on price; the form Otter heard as "L3 and eight" still holds a premium on cognition; "popularity is the death knell on premium" [00:20].
- NAD+ escaped niche last year and grew three times on the US shelf in 18 months; stacks with spermidine and resveratrol won back some premium in 2026, but it is near price war [00:20].
- Postbiotics are growing fast, have "really strong connections into GLP-1" and earn one of the strongest premiums; he is watching them most closely [00:20].
- Men do not buy into an andropause label; they respond to testosterone, performance and prostate messages [00:20].
- A brand Otter heard as "I am eight" broke 100 million in year one, is on target for 220 to 230 in year two, projects 400 million in year three and raised a billion in funding on a profitable subscription model; he named it and "ancient and brave" as brands nailing proof [00:20].
- Positioning that facilitates "someone's perfect life" lasts longer than solving a problem, which ends when it is fixed or fails; collagen can be sold either way [00:20].
- Takeaways: lead with proof; know the ingredient's life stage and the pipeline behind it; segment and price, with women heading into perimenopause badly served; and design proof for three gatekeepers: shoppers, healthcare professionals and agentic commerce [00:20].
summary.For Vita Actives: His timing for relief on premium whey supply, late 2027 at the earliest, shows how long sports protein brands' margins may stay squeezed [00:20]; Alan Johnstone's new US and European capacity at SANS Europe ran to 2028 (unfiltered-an-insider-s-view-of); my reading is that this keeps the door open for IsoClr: Pea in blends through 2027. His ingredient life cycle applies to creatine: proof brings a premium and popularity erodes it [00:20]; my reading is that CreaWin's case to brands should rest on its own evidence and a clear benefit, not on creatine's popularity. Healthy-ageing customers pay for named needs and proof, and in Europe mitochondrial wording is already established [00:20]; my reading is that our healthy-ageing pitches should name the need and the evidence. His point that AI shopping agents read proof differently means our evidence files should be structured and machine-readable (my reading). Relevance high: healthy-ageing market structure and sports protein economics.

summary.Summary: Nick Morgan (Nutrition Integrated) opened the day by arguing that the principles of sports nutrition have gone further, rather than sports nutrition itself going mainstream, and put three questions to the room: is the category growing beyond the motivations that defined it, is it winning consumers while losing its identity, and is the market growing or are the boundaries just moving [00:00] (photo 31). His three rules were that growth does not guarantee value, relevance does not guarantee ownership, and opportunity does not guarantee advantage [00:00]. The evidence was Starbucks' 15 g protein cold foam (Starbucks say one in seven coffees now carries 15 g of protein), whey protein at historically high prices (WPI at EUR 30.5 a kilogram and WPC80 at EUR 27.6 by July 2026, about fourfold on 2023, on Vesper's index) and the brand responses to it (fewer promotions, 1 kg packs cut to 900 g at the same price, reformulation, "whey hybrids", whey milkshakes, whey plus collagen at 10 g plus 10 g), creatine moving into gummies, chocolate and products for women, and a hydration market with no agreed electrolyte dose [00:00] (photo 4) (photo 6) (photo 18). He showed the scale of competition from Nutrition Integrated's tracking of 16,412 product listings across the US and Europe: 3,448 creatine products, 2,833 magnesium and 2,648 collagen, with branded ingredients in 53% of pre-workouts, 40% of longevity products and 25% of creatine products [00:00], [18:50] (photo 23) (photo 27). He closed on four principles (think beyond the category, stay true to your DNA, choose where to compete, know your right to win) and on "permission to play" and the right to win: everyone has a seat at the table, but not everyone will win [18:50] (photo 32).
summary.Key takeaways:
- Starbucks' protein cold foam (15 g) started in Q4 2025 in America and is now in the UK, Central Europe, Singapore and India; Starbucks say one in seven coffees currently provides 15 g of protein. "A bigger market does not simply mean more of the same market." [00:00]
- Raw whey prices: on Vesper's EU index, WPI rose from about EUR 11 a kilogram in January 2023 to EUR 30.5 by July 2026 and WPC80 from about EUR 7 to EUR 27.6, while WPC35 moved only from about EUR 3 to EUR 4.3; the slide calls it "the strongest period of price inflation on record", with WPC80 and WPI up about fourfold on 2023 and the sharpest acceleration in H1 2026 [00:00] (photo 4).
- Whey protein prices have never been higher and brands are going through a "structural reset", not mitigation: fewer promotions, pack architecture (1 kg to 900 g at the same price), some reformulation, a rush of new whey launches, and a push to sell higher-margin lines instead. Consumer prices per kilogram for priority brands in Europe rose between October 2025 and October 2026 by 13.6% for clear whey (EUR 60.14 to 68.32), 28.0% for HWP/WPI (47.73 to 61.10), 28.8% for whey blends (37.56 to 48.38), 15.0% for whey hybrids (35.64 to 40.97) and 20.8% for WPC (36.66 to 44.29); he said 15 to 25 percent from the stage. He believes protein will "look quite differently in 18 to 20 months" [00:00] (photo 8).
- His mitigation ladder has six rungs: price increases (widespread), reduced promotion (increasingly common) and pack architecture (widely adopted globally) are tactical; reformulation is strategic and brand specific; new products that cut whey reliance and a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre are the "top priority for brands", with the limitations named as a ground-zero revenue base, brand permission and alienating core consumers [00:00] (photo 6).
- Brands "would love to listen to you about some really good solutions": they want to sell more creatine, electrolytes, pre-workout and higher-value vitamins because the margin structure is better than whey [00:00].
- "Whey hybrids" (presented as whey, blended with milk, soy or yeast to cut cost of goods) launched in greater numbers in the last 12 months than ever; whey milkshakes (whey plus milk) and whey plus collagen (typically 10 g plus 10 g, in shakes and clear drinks) are the next pillars; GLP-1 and longevity proteins, yeast, mycelium and air-derived protein are coming through but are still expensive [00:00]. The slide's examples were Bulk Daily Whey Protein ("best value protein"), Myprotein's Impact Whey Protein Milkshake (20 g protein, 2.6 g sugar, 1.2 g fat per 29 g serving), Clean Simple Eats Protein Powder + Collagen and Planta (20 g protein, 24 vitamins and minerals, 1,000 mg BCAAs) (photo 9).
- Six "pillars of innovation" from the price squeeze: whey choice risks confusing consumers; communications react more than they solve; hybrid powders are gaining consistency (dairy plus plant in overt blends); caseinate is the new milkshake; plant protein still needs a taste breakthrough; and the Myprotein x Nero launch signals a race for the next cafe collaboration [00:00] (photo 12).
- Plant protein is not taking the gap: ranges come in and out because they still underdeliver on taste. The winning message is "we're just a really bloody good protein", not "plant"; dairy plus plant hybrids are appearing for the first time and caseinates are gaining with milk volatility [00:00]. His example was Rocka's vegan range: Pro Protein at 24 g protein, 122 kcal, an 83% fava bean and pea blend, EUR 37.99 per 700 g (EUR 1.65 a serve); Natural Protein at 21 g, 112 kcal, 86.6% soy, fava, almond and pea, EUR 29.99 per 600 g (EUR 1.50 a serve); Protein Shake, "the tastiest vegan protein powder", 84% blend, EUR 37.99 per 900 g (EUR 1.27 a serve), plant moving "from an extended product proposition to a simple product attribute" (photo 10).
- The creatine benchmark is Optimum Nutrition's Micronised Creatine Powder: 3 g creatine monohydrate a serve, GBP 14.00 for the 187 g unflavoured tub (25p a serve, EUR 0.33) and GBP 16.00 for 247 g flavoured (29p a serve), fronted by Lauren James, Chelsea and England footballer (photo 13).
- Creatine is now "for all people and for all occasions"; gummies are the fastest-growing format by new launches in the last six months, off a small base, with "lots of conjecture about stability"; "other" formats (liquids, foods, chocolate) grew faster still off a tiny base, and most brands now have a route into broader retail [00:00], [25:59]. The format split of 2,639 creatine products: powder 70.1% (13.1% added in the last six months), capsule 17.0% (8.7%), gummy 8.0% (36.2%), tablet 4.2% (14.4%), effervescent 0.4% (10.0%), other 0.3% (44.4%); 378 products, 14.3% of the total, were added in six months. The examples were Creatonics' "Creatine+ formulated for women" sachet and Sunday Natural's Nutrachoc creatine chocolate (20 pieces at 1,000 mg creatine monohydrate, sweetened with tagatose) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- Hydration: no agreed electrolyte dose (SiS "all five essential", LMNT 1,000 mg sodium, Precision by sweat rate); Liquid IV is the category leader at £1.50 a stick; effervescents are three times cheaper than a stick pack; naturalness (no colours or preservatives, natural sweeteners and flavours, short ingredient lists) is a prerequisite to growth [00:00]. The shelf prices on the slide: Liquid I.V. GBP 1.50 a sachet (GBP 9.00 for 6; GBP 1.00 on Clubcard), Phizz GBP 0.40 a tablet (GBP 8.00 for 20; GBP 0.28 on Clubcard), Evian 750 ml GBP 1.85 single, Red Bull 250 ml GBP 2.10 single, Lucozade Sport 500 ml GBP 1.65 single (photo 16).
- Declared sodium a serve on selected electrolyte powders runs from 38 mg (ViDrate Boost) through 350 mg (SiS Hydro+), 500 mg (Cadence Daily), 570 mg (Liquid I.V. Multiplier) and 750 mg (Hunter & Gather) to 1,000 mg (LMNT); 69% of powders include four or five electrolytes, and 8% of products claim Himalayan sea salt as a natural sodium source. The slide's heading: "there is no optimal formula" [00:00] (photo 18).
- Hydration powders are positioned three ways: everyday hydration (Humantra, Hunter & Gather, Repowr: routine, natural, sugar-free), superior hydration (SOS "4x faster than water", Ancient + Brave, ARTAH "cellular hydration") and performance hydration (226ERS Hydra Zero on sweat losses, HIGH5 Isotonic carbs plus electrolytes, Precision PH strength options) (photo 22).
- Naturalness in ingredient declarations: 40% state natural colours, 46% use natural flavours and 43% include stevia; Humantra names grape skin as its colour source, Liquid I.V. declares sugar alongside steviol glycosides, ViDrate covers flavour, colour and sweetening in one proposition and Cadence extends the absence message to fillers [00:00] (photo 24).
- Product counts tracked (US and Europe, 16,412 listings across eight spaces): 3,448 creatine (new-product activity +10% over the latest six months), 2,833 magnesium (+15%), 2,648 collagen, 2,153 energy and focus, 1,869 pre-workout, 1,626 sleep and mood, 1,487 electrolyte and 348 longevity (+20% new); he said almost 3,500 creatine, almost 2,800 magnesium and over 2,500 collagen from the stage. "Only a few will be really successful", by pulling on format, brand, dose, science and branded solutions [00:00] (photo 23).
- Branded ingredient penetration (share of tracked products with at least one identified branded ingredient): pre-workout 53% (many use more than one), longevity 40%, energy and focus 31%, sleep and mood 25%, creatine 25%, collagen 25%, electrolyte 17%, magnesium 17%; in creatine most comes from one supplier and "there's a race for those to follow". His slide's nuance: minerals "need to work harder to prove the benefit" [18:50] (photo 27).
- Longevity products take three approaches: alter the ageing process (cellular health, mitochondria, senescence), optimise the ageing experience (muscle and mobility, cognition, energy, sleep) or personalise to a life stage (ageing athletes, menopause, later life); Cellaro's Vitalize AM, Renew PM and Reset monthly range against the 12 hallmarks of ageing was the example [18:50] (photo 29).
- Longevity brands and athlete-backed brands (Sergio Ramos linking sport to longevity through Centenarian: "Real longevity, backed by science. To perform better. To live better.") compete for the same consumer with sports nutrition products framed as "live better today"; the competitive set has never been broader [18:50] (photo 30).
- Brands must think beyond the category (gut, longevity, GLP-1) but stay true to the industry's DNA, choose where to compete and understand the right to win; this will be "the biggest challenge you face for your budgets and strategy in 2027 and beyond" [18:50].
- The four closing principles: think beyond the category (new consumers, needs and occasions); stay true to your DNA (capabilities, credibility, differentiation); choose where to compete ("where you could play from where you should play"); know your right to win (where you can create distinctive value). "Growth creates opportunity. Understanding change creates advantage." [18:50] (photo 32)
summary.For Vita Actives: Whey margin pressure is the strongest tailwind in the talk for an ingredient supplier: brands are actively looking for higher-margin, non-whey lines and for new protein blends, and he told the room they want to hear solutions [00:00]; his own slide lists a portfolio shift into creatine, energy and fibre as a "top priority for brands" (photo 6). For CreaWin: creatine is his benchmark category, 25% of 3,448 products use a branded ingredient, most of it from one supplier, and he said there is a race to follow [18:50] (photo 27); my reading is that this is exactly the gap a second branded creatine pitches into, with science and story as the differentiators he named. Gummies (8.0% of products, 36.2% added in six months) and food formats are where creatine launches are growing and stability is the open question [00:00] (photo 14); my reading is that a stability story for CreaWin in gummies would land with brands. The ON benchmark sets the consumer price floor at 25p a serve for 3 g (photo 13). For IsoClr: Pea: his point that plant protein must be sold as a very good protein rather than as plant, and that taste is the barrier, fits a clear pea isolate pitched on taste and clarity first (my reading); Rocka's range shows fava and pea blends sold at EUR 1.27 to 1.65 a serve (photo 10). The whey hybrid and whey plus collagen trend shows brands will blend protein sources, including in clear drinks, which opens room for a pea component in clear formats (my reading). For Oxystorm: pre-workout has the highest branded-ingredient penetration, 53%, so it is crowded but receptive to branded actives (photo 27) (my reading). Naturalness and short ingredient lists are a prerequisite across the board [00:00] (photo 24). Relevance high: it is the market-structure and protein-pricing frame for everything else at this event.

summary.Summary: Alan Johnstone (owner of Nutrilution, formerly selling whey at Arla Foods Ingredients) explained the supply chain behind this year's whey prices [00:16]. On Vesper's EU index WPI rose from a trough of about EUR 7 a kilogram in 2023 to EUR 32.00 on 25 August 2026, and WPC80, up roughly sixfold since 2020, jumped from about 12 euros to 28 in about six weeks, which hurt more because brands had already switched into WPC80 [00:16] (photo 2) (photo 16). Demand is growing at over 10% a year (sports nutrition, GLP-1 users, mainstream protein, clear whey, which is almost all WPI), while liquid whey only grows with cheese production at about 1.5% a year, and filtration plants are expensive and slow to build [00:16] (photo 7). Over five years producers grew WPI at 15.0% a year (80,494 t in 2020 to 161,800 t in 2025) and WPC80 at 1.5% (334,000 t to 360,000 t); new capacity suggests WPI at 7 to 11% and WPC80 at 4 to 7% a year to 2030, but not both at the top [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 11). Prices overshoot in both directions on buyer behaviour, and between 25 August and 4 November 2026 WPC80 fell 40.7% to EUR 16.00 a kilogram and WPI 20.3% to EUR 25.50, while MPC85 rose 13.5% to EUR 15.80 and met WPC80 [00:16] (photo 18). His advice: do not try to time the bottom, keep buying steadily if the price lets you make money, and accept that whey "will be expensive. It should be expensive" [00:16] (photo 20).
summary.Key takeaways:
- WPI went from around 7 euros a kilogram in 2023 to over 30 euros earlier this year; WPC80 held around 12 euros, then rocketed to 28 in about six weeks. WPC80 was the existential risk for brands because they had already moved their sourcing into it [00:16]. The slide puts WPI near EUR 32 a kilogram at the summer record and WPC80 up roughly sixfold since 2020, both "now correcting"; its chart (Vesper, EU monthly, December 2019 to October 2026) shows WPC80 at about EUR 5 in 2020 and 2023, peaking about EUR 12 in 2022 and about EUR 26 to 27 in mid 2026, and WPI at about EUR 8 in 2020, EUR 18 in 2022, EUR 7 in 2023 and about EUR 31 in mid 2026 (photo 2).
- Demand drivers: traditional sports nutrition at 10% a year on Euromonitor, which he thinks is a big underestimate; GLP-1 users as incremental demand; protein going mainstream (Starbucks, Papa John's, Dunkin'); clear whey, which barely existed five years ago, is one of the fastest-selling parts of the category and is almost all whey [00:16]. The slide's figures: the 2024 global sports nutrition market splits 48% protein powders, 26% protein bars, 17% non-protein and 9% protein RTD, growing 8 to 10% a year; clear whey SKUs are up 35% year on year; 12% of US adults take a GLP-1 medication, with protein spend up 20% (KFF 2025, BCG 2026); Starbucks' protein drinks carry 15 to 36 g (photo 3).
- Whey wins on taste and texture, not nutrition: "the more mainstream you get with protein products, the less people care about the protein source." It is far easier to make a good-tasting product with whey than with most alternatives [00:16].
- Supply: only 0.6% of liquid milk is whey protein (the rest by weight: water 87.3%, lactose 4.7%, fat 3.9%, casein 2.8%, minerals 0.7%); whey comes from cheese, and cheese production grows about 1.5% a year, so liquid whey does too, against demand growing over 10%. This is his most important conclusion [00:16] (photo 4) (photo 7).
- The route from milk: cheese keeps the casein and fat; liquid whey goes through ultrafiltration and drying to WPC (35 to 80% protein), microfiltration or ion exchange to WPI (90% or more), then acidification or hydrolysis to clear or hydrolysed WPI; each step is a plant, and sweet whey powder (about 12% protein), permeate, lactose, demineralised whey (D70, D90, for infant nutrition) and whey cream are the other outlets for the same whey [00:16] (photo 4).
- Factories are the first bottleneck ("phenomenally expensive" and slow to build; the slide: "CAPEX intensive, less flexible than people expect, takes years to start commercial production"); liquid whey is the second; byproducts are the third, "a major influencer of producer value", and WPI producers must also sell a fatty protein stream [00:16] (photo 6) (photo 7).
- Over five years total whey protein supply grew just under 5% a year: global WPC80 plus WPI production rose 26%, from 414,494 t in 2020 to 521,800 t in 2025 (a 4.7% CAGR); WPI grew 15.0% a year (80,494 t to 161,800 t) at the expense of WPC80 at 1.5% (334,000 t to 360,000 t), which explains why WPC80 was undersupplied this year. Clear whey may be up to 25% of WPI (top of the estimate range; 40,450 t of the 161,800 t in 2025); ordinary instant WPI grew 8.6% a year, below the category [00:16] (photo 8) (photo 9).
- New capacity: WPI expected to grow 7 to 11% a year, WPC80 4 to 7% (CAGR 2025 to 2030), but if WPI is at 11, WPC80 has to be more like 4 because there is not enough whey. Both are below underlying demand [00:16] (photo 11).
- The capacity list: announced US additions (McCully Consulting, approximate) of 24,400 t of WPC80 and 7,500 t of WPI in 2026, 41,600 t and 20,300 t in 2027, 45,900 t and 22,900 t in 2028; in the UK, EU and Oceania, FrieslandCampina (WPI expansion), Fonterra (various speciality) and Polmlek (WPC and WPI) in 2026, Tirlan (WPC, WPI and clear) and Liprovit (WPI) in 2027, and Arla's mozzarella plant in 2028. He said the European list is not exhaustive, with some Eastern European producers he could not get information from [00:16] (photo 11).
- Prices overshoot on behaviour, in both directions (the COVID example): buyers stock up when prices rise and sit out when they fall. The slide's cycle: longer lead times, inventory, demand rises, buyers compete for available material, prices rise, incentive to buy early, demand rises again, with the brand and consumer response feeding back into demand; the 2022 peak was logistics freeing up and buyers destocking, the 2023 trough buyers waiting as long as possible with stocks too low [00:16] (photo 13) (photo 15).
- Now: WPC80 "has been falling pretty hard", WPI "still expensive, but definitely correcting"; new US factories set in motion three or four years ago are commissioning; producers have better uses for whey (WPI, WPC35, sweet whey powder), so WPC80 production should fall; MPC85 and other substitutes are rising and WPC80 and milk protein lines "should never meet" [00:16]. The weekly Vesper figures: between 25 August and 4 November 2026 WPC80 fell 40.7%, from EUR 27.00 to EUR 16.00 a kilogram, WPI fell 20.3%, from EUR 32.00 to EUR 25.50, and MPC85 rose 13.5%, from EUR 13.92 to EUR 15.80, meeting WPC80 at about EUR 16 on 4 November (photo 16) (photo 18).
- The MPC85 line: brands substituted MPC85 (or MPI, caseins, plant proteins) into formulations, so those prices are rising while WPC80 falls; he quoted Keynes on markets staying irrational longer than you can stay solvent, so the lines touching does not mean they bounce apart at once, "but it can't go on forever" [00:16] (photo 18).
- What decides the next move, from the slide: for WPC80 the bullish forces are strong other derivatives, rising alternatives and long-term protein demand, the bearish ones high inventories, powerful momentum and demand destruction; for WPI, bullish are its smaller share of brand costs, healthy inventories on both sides and being harder to replace, bearish are demand destruction and production increases due (photo 16).
- Where prices go: "structurally rising but volatile"; the correction is under way and "may overshoot below trend... then demand pulls it back up". The schematic averages EU WPC80 and WPI (Vesper, monthly to October 2026) and the slide says the trend and forward path are "directional, not a forecast" [00:16] (photo 19).
- Advice: do not try to be too clever with volume; buy steadily if the price works; whey will be and should be expensive; a business that cannot cope with this year's prices needs to change its model [00:16]. The three closing takeaways on the slide: "Don't try to time the market. Keep inventory steady. Whey will be expensive." (photo 20)
- Nutrilution also sells niche, higher-value ingredients and advises buyers on whey and dairy protein sourcing, including cross-continental supply chains [00:16].
summary.For Vita Actives: The structural case for non-dairy protein is made by a whey insider: cheese grows 1.5% a year and demand over 10%, and he expects whey to stay expensive [00:16] (photo 7) (photo 20). For IsoClr: Pea, my reading is that this is the opening, but he also set the bar: mainstream consumers care about taste and texture, not source, and whey is the easiest protein to make taste good, so a clear pea isolate has to win on taste and clarity before it wins on supply. Nick Morgan's observation that brands want higher-margin non-protein lines applies here too: CreaWin and Oxystorm are the lines brands want to grow while whey margins are thin (my reading). Nutrilution is a potential partner or competitor in niche ingredients and sourcing advice. Relevance high: protein market structure and pricing.

summary.Summary: Nikki Hancocks (NutraIngredients) chaired a panel on how brands build communities online while regulators watch, opening with an NI report of more than 1,000 misleading food communication posts by influencers, supplements the most frequent subject [00:01]. Sinead Gibbons (Tonic Health) said 99% of Tonic's content is not about its products: the "Unsponsored Truth" supermarket swaps have built 1.9 million followers and about 70 million views a month, run by one 22-year-old social media manager and a freelance editor [01:00], [14:35]. Julian Harvie (AG1) said too much evidence fails at the top of the funnel, that AG1 practises "restraint", and that Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version" and "a slightly better version" before approving "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" [04:17], [18:30]. Dan Richardson (nutritionist) said athletes want the headline, not the numbers, that buzzwords with different connotations from the research are the common slip, and that athletes are the most impressionable audience of all [06:30], [08:33], [32:33]. Luca Bucchini (for ESSNA) listed the rules (the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules, a new digital act coming) and the recurring failures: undisclosed ads, strategies built around non-compliance, and following non-compliant discourse; brands bear most responsibility for influencer claims [09:45], [11:59], [28:27]. On AI, Julian's rule is that the idea must begin and end with a human [35:43].
summary.Key takeaways:
- More than 1,000 misleading food communication posts by influencers were counted in a recent report, with supplements the most frequent subject [00:01].
- Tonic's model is "a media business that happens to sell vitamins": 20 to 30 second clips, three posts a day, 1.9 million followers, about 70 million views a month, 99% of content not about the product; people come to social "to be educated or to be entertained" [01:00], [03:24].
- Tonic posts 900 pieces of content a month across four channels with a team of one social media manager and a freelance editor; after the ASA pulled up a profile cover claiming "the best sleep supplement in the market" for its magnesium drink, every element now goes through an AI compliance agent [14:35].
- Tonic never deletes a challenged post: it changes the caption, answers the comments, sends voice notes and makes response videos, because "trust is really built in those small moments" [14:35].
- AG1 found that talking about gold-standard trials and third-party testing did not land: "people didn't care". Too much evidence does not work top of funnel; the science sits mid-funnel for people in the consideration set [04:17], [18:30].
- Clearcast rejected "the best version of you", "a better version of you" and "a slightly better version of you"; the approved line was "Ever wondered what life would be like with a little extra help?" Julian's lesson: "creative constraint is a very powerful way to deliver better communication" [18:30].
- AG1 cannot associate healthcare professionals, dietitians or doctors directly with the brand, so it uses them for pure education ("what is creatine? Like, how does it work?", "why is magnesium important?") and hopes the credibility transfers [22:46].
- Dan: athletes want the headline backed by research; the common slip is swapping dull research words for buzzwords whose connotations differ, often "genuine accidental misleading"; "what you can and can't say around a product is a massive gray area" [06:30], [08:33].
- Dan is food first: he told a creatine company's podcast audience that not everybody should take creatine until the baseline of nutrition is fixed, and the company objected [24:22].
- Athletes are "probably the most impressionable group": a 35-year-old EFL player with 200-plus appearances bought a supplement off TikTok Shop; they believe "up to 10% better performance" applies to them personally [32:33].
- Luca: the rules are the nutrition and health claims regulation, the UK advertising codes, member state influencer rules and a new digital act whose text is not yet known; failures are undisclosed ads, no training or allocated responsibility with creators, strategies built around non-compliance, and following a non-compliant discourse [09:45], [11:59].
- Brands bear most responsibility for influencers' health claims in most jurisdictions; the answer is training, contracts and briefing [28:27].
- Provocation without a solution is fearmongering: Tonic will not post a call-out unless it gives the healthier swap [30:18].
- AI: Julian's hard rule is that "the idea has to begin and end with a human being"; AI scales the middle; he found human copy still better by some margin. Luca expects regulatory action as consumers take nutrition advice from AI agents; AI is also used by regulators to monitor posts [35:43], [38:28], [39:48].
summary.For Vita Actives: Our customers' marketing teams are under claims pressure from the ASA, Clearcast and the claims regulation, and the panel's answer was education content that does not sell: "what is creatine, how does it work" is exactly what AG1 makes with its experts [22:46]. My reading is that a branded ingredient earns its place by giving brands substantiated, claim-safe education they can publish, in the headline-plus-evidence form Dan described, not by giving them stronger claims. For CreaWin, Dan's food-first framing (creatine after the baseline is fixed) and the athlete anecdotes show creatine is already a mainstay in the eyes of athletes and nutritionists [24:22], [32:33]; my reading is that our creatine content should be calm and educational, and wording we supply to brands must survive an ASA review. Luca's point that brands carry the liability for what influencers say means brands will want suppliers' claims to be referenced and hedged exactly [28:27]. Relevance medium: marketing and regulation, adjacent to our ingredients.

summary.Summary: James Morton (Science in Sport) argued that the biggest barrier to fuelling the female runner is educational, not biological [00:00] (photo 20). From a 2021 Medicine and Science in Sports and Exercise study of recreational runners with muscle biopsies before and after three sessions, women started with less muscle glycogen than men but finished the same; the gap was under 5 g in the gastrocnemius and disappears when the same absolute carbohydrate is given, so it does not change practical guidance [00:00]. In an England Athletics study of elite runners (marathon bests about 2:20 for men and 2:40 for women) fed 60, 90 or 120 g of carbohydrate an hour over a two-hour run (15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint, 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold), 120 g prevented the crossover from carbohydrate to fat in both sexes, exogenous oxidation reached about 1 g a minute at 60 g, 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g and some individuals oxidised 80 to 100 percent of what they took at 120 g, and running economy improved by two to 3% in both sexes; the male data is Ravikanti et al. (2025) in the Journal of Applied Physiology and the female data is under revision [00:00] (photo 2) (photo 6) (photo 7). He showed a fuelling framework from Morton et al. (2026) in the Journal of Nutrition that sets carbohydrate by intensity and duration, from none for an easy hour to 120 g an hour dual source for a marathon, and described the SiS partnership with Nike's After Dark Tour as an education programme in seven cities with a co-branded race pack and a range "designed for her" [00:00] (photo 12) (photo 17) (photo 19). He does not believe in fuelling to the menstrual cycle: treat the female athlete as an athlete first [00:00] (photo 20). In the Q&A he said power analysis supports nine participants, fat-free mass may be the better dosing basis for women, and dual-source blends are needed at 90 and 120 g but not below 90 minutes [22:54], [23:48], [24:34], [25:17].
summary.Key takeaways:
- In the 2021 study (recreational runners, 6 g per kg carbohydrate on the day, a 10-mile run at lactate threshold, 8 x 800 m, 3 x 10 minutes), women began with less muscle glycogen than men but both finished similarly depleted; the difference was less than 5 g in the gastrocnemius and has no practical bearing on guidelines [00:00].
- The gap is a dosing artefact: carbohydrate is prescribed per kilogram, so lighter women take less in absolute terms; given the same absolute amount, "there isn't really any differences in glycogen storage". His hedge: for a given relative intake women "may present with slightly less absolute glycogen" [00:00].
- Study design: 8 g per kg carbohydrate on day one, a 2 g per kg breakfast on day two, then 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold, 90 minutes at 94% of lactate turnpoint (simulated race pace) and 15 minutes at 95% of lactate threshold; the 60 g an hour condition was maltodextrin only, the 90 and 120 g conditions 1:1 maltodextrin and fructose [00:00] (photo 2).
- Elite runners (men about 2:20, women about 2:40 marathon bests) ran two hours after 8 g per kg the day before and 2 g per kg at breakfast; 60 g an hour gave a crossover to fat after about 60 minutes, 90 g shifted it right, 120 g prevented it for the full two hours [00:00]. The slides show the crossover at about 60 to 75 minutes on 60 g in both sexes and no crossover on 120 g in either, with men's carbohydrate oxidation on 120 g holding at about 3.0 to 3.2 g a minute from 45 to 105 minutes (photo 3) (photo 4) (photo 6).
- Exogenous oxidation (carbon-13): about 1 g a minute at 60 g an hour, close to 1.3 to 1.4 at 90 g, and at 120 g some men and women oxidised between 80 and 100 percent of intake, "some of the highest rates of oxidation ever reported"; men and women do not differ in ability to digest and oxidise carbohydrate [00:00]. The slide's peak means, read from the chart: men about 1.0, 1.5 and 1.8 g a minute at 60, 90 and 120 g; women about 1.0, 1.45 and 1.75; seven to eight participants a group; "120 > 90 > 60 g" in both sexes (photo 7).
- Running economy improved by between two and 3% at 120 g an hour, against Nike's 4% Vaporfly claim; he is "pretty sure" this is part of why running records are falling [00:00]. The conclusion slide: 120 g an hour "reduces the oxygen cost of running (i.e. improves running economy) compared with traditional CHO guidelines of 60-90 g/h" (photo 9).
- Women reported more gastrointestinal symptoms than men, "which may be due to anatomical differences in colon length"; tolerance may differ slightly, oxidation does not [00:00]. The slide's wording: "individual variations in rates of exogenous CHO oxidation and gastrointestinal symptoms warrant CHO personalisation strategies" (photo 9).
- Fuelling matrix (Journal of Nutrition): an easy 60-minute run needs no carbohydrate; 60 minutes at higher intensity 30 to 60 g an hour; team sport or half marathon towards 90 g; two to three hours a definite rationale for 120 g. Ultra-endurance (three to eight hours) is the gap SiS's science strategy will work on [00:00].
- The framework in full (Morton et al. 2026, Journal of Nutrition) plots intensity (zones 1 to 5; moderate under 2 mmol/L, heavy 2 to 4, severe over 4) against duration: under an hour, 0 g, 0 to 30 g or 30 to 60 g single source for HIT (mouth rinse, drinks, gels); one to two hours, 30 to 60 g single source, 60 to 90 g single or dual source for soccer, 90 g dual source for a half marathon (drinks, gels, chews); two to three hours, 60 to 90 g single or dual, 90 to 120 g dual, 120 g dual source for a marathon (drinks, gels, chews, bars); beyond three hours cycling stages, beyond six ultra (photo 12).
- The barriers: female marathoners "do not know the numbers" (psychological capability; participant 18 took her first gel at 7 or 8 miles and went by what others do) and tolerating carbohydrate during a race can be a barrier (physical capability; participant 13 aimed for about 80 g an hour, felt her stomach "was not happy" in the heat and skipped her last two gels); like men, female runners need to practise fuelling in training (photo 13) (photo 14) (photo 15).
- SiS partnered with Nike After Dark (women's night races in seven cities) on education rather than product creation, with co-branded products by race duration; the partnership continues [00:00]. The Sydney 21K race pack sells at $40.00 ("Fuel your night"): eight packs of Run Fuel Endurance energy gels (3 x 60 ml), Run Hydro+ electrolyte powder (4.3 g), a Run Fuel Endurance energy chew (50 g) and Run Recovery Endurance powder (73 g) (photo 17).
- The Nike x SiS After Dark range, "designed for her", laid out for 10K and half marathon: Run Fuel Isotonic gel (22 g single-source carbohydrate; before and during), Run Fuel Endurance gel (40 g dual source; during), Run Fuel Endurance chew (40 g dual source, 1:0.8 glucose to fructose; before and during), Run Hydro+ sugar-free electrolytes (350 mg sodium; before, during and after), Run Recovery (25 g single-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) and Run Recovery Endurance (40 g dual-source carbohydrate, 25 g protein including 5 g collagen; after) (photo 19).
- "The biggest barrier to fueling the female runner is not biological... it is educational"; under-fuelling is cultural; he does not believe in day-of-cycle fuelling messages [00:00]. The closing slide: the barrier "is not likely a biological limitation i.e. their gut or their muscles" but "lack of knowledge and awareness of the guidelines", in "a world where under-fuelling has been prevalent"; fuelling "is less about hormones and tailoring to the menstrual cycle, put simply, it is about fuelling for the work required" (photo 20).
- Q&A: nine participants gives 80% power because a 30 g step changes oxidation by 0.3 to 0.4 g a minute [22:54]; women should probably be dosed per kilogram of fat-free mass, but it is hard to measure [23:48]; 60 g was maltodextrin only, 90 and 120 g dual source; dual source is needed above about 90 minutes and lowers oxidation at 60 g [24:34], [25:17].
summary.For Vita Actives: Nothing in the talk touches our ingredients: no protein, creatine or pre-workout was mentioned from the stage, and the only protein on a slide is the 25 g (including 5 g collagen) in the two Run Recovery drinks of the Nike x SiS range, source not stated (photo 19). The value is customer insight: SiS builds its pitch on its own trials (England Athletics, Nike), published papers and a one-slide framework, and its chief science voice is openly sceptical of claims he sees on social media [00:00] (photo 12). My reading is that a sports nutrition brand of this kind expects a supplier to bring trial data and a one-slide rule of thumb, not a benefit list, and that is the standard CreaWin and IsoClr: Pea material should meet. The gut tolerance point (more GI symptoms in women at high intakes, and a runner skipping gels on an unhappy stomach) is adjacent to the digestibility story for a clear pea protein (photo 15) (my reading). The clear recovery drinks carry 25 g protein in a clear format for women runners, which is the format IsoClr: Pea is made for (my reading). Relevance low: carbohydrate fuelling, outside our range.

summary.Summary: Olivia Haslam (NutraIngredients) talked with Marchon's founder Ollie Marchon and head of product Liam Holmes about what the rise of the "everyday athlete" means for sports nutrition [00:00]. Ollie split these consumers into three groups (inspired by, driven by, live by) and said most of their 8,000 daily app users train at 6:00 in the morning, which changes what they need [00:54]. Liam argued for "situational" formats, such as carbohydrate in a pre-workout for people who cannot eat at 6 a.m. [04:00]. Ollie said awareness of ingredients and supplements is high but understanding lags, so education, honest positioning and efficacious doses matter [05:29] [18:39]. They see creatine as here to stay, moving into cognition, with format and stability as the challenge for ingredient suppliers [08:24]. Their five-year bet is formats that improve compliance [22:11].
summary.Key takeaways:
- The everyday athlete: the running boom, Hyrox ("high rocks" in Otter) and strength training have blurred the line between elite athletes and everyone else [00:54] [03:05].
- Three segments: "inspired by" (habits, feeling better, multivitamin, omega, sleep, food first), driven by ("The driven buy" in Otter; measured progress, nutrient timing before, during and after training) and "live by" (optimisers who plan the whole 24 hours around training) [00:54].
- Timing: most of their 8,000 daily training-app users train at 6:00 in the morning, as do most gym members; they are in a different fed state from people who trained after work before COVID [00:54].
- Situational formats: Marchon put carbohydrate into a pre-workout ("workout fuel") because people training at 5 or 6 a.m. do not want to eat toast or porridge first [04:00].
- Awareness is high, understanding lags: gym-goers talk confidently about products they saw in an ad or from influencers without knowing why, so "education is really critical at this stage" [05:29].
- Creatine needed little brand communication: they rode the wave of big podcast voices on longevity, healthspan and healthy ageing, and of its "decades of of literature"; it builds the daily supplement ritual and mixes into squash, water or porridge [06:53].
- Liam: creatine is "here to stay", the research is moving into cognition and possibly recovery, and for ingredient suppliers the challenge is format: stability in water, in gummies and in other formats [08:24].
- Opportunity areas: gut health, immunity, sleep and recovery, as people train harder, longer and across modalities; gut health to absorb higher carbohydrate loads is "still something that's untapped" [09:36].
- Discipline over hype: Ollie cited a stat of "2005" electrolyte brands launched last year and said marketing electrolytes as fuel in place of carbohydrate is "a bit of a miss"; low-sodium electrolytes to drink more water through the day are fine [11:15] [13:09].
- Liam prefers established ingredients reaching new uses as research catches up (creatine for cognition, curcumin, certain probiotics) over "the new shiny ingredient" [14:05].
- Claims: communicating the benefit is "a regulatory nightmare"; Marchon attaches ingredients to formats already in a routine, such as a creatine plus multivitamin or a "Brain Health Plus multivitamin" [15:23].
- When Marchon surveyed its gym members, the number one struggle was still hitting their daily protein requirement; many marathon runners weeks from the race had not tried a gel [16:50].
- Dose matters: a magnesium product for sleep without the right amount gives no benefit, and disappointed first-time buyers move on to the next trend [18:39].
- Compliance: Amazon now sets more hoops than TikTok Shop; YouTube channels, regulators and third-party lab testing are catching up with poor practice; Science in Sport's chief science officer and advisory boards are the model [20:29] [21:13].
- Five years out: "formats that improve compliance" (gummies, jellies, powders, RTDs) and convenience [22:11].
- Ingredient supply, prices or sourcing were not discussed; the only supplier point was the creatine format challenge [08:24] (my reading).
summary.For Vita Actives: For CreaWin, this is a brand saying out loud what it wants from a creatine supplier: stability in water, in gummies and in new formats [08:24]. My reading is that stability data in those formats is the conversation opener with brands like Marchon. Creatine also works as the entry ritual for new supplement users and pairs with products already in a routine (creatine plus multivitamin) [06:53] [15:23]; my reading is that combination concepts are worth pitching. The top struggle among Marchon's gym members is hitting daily protein [16:50], which keeps the protein base growing; my reading is that convenient, early-morning formats are where a clear pea protein like IsoClr: Pea could fit. Early-morning training and carbohydrate in pre-workout is a pre-workout reformulation trend relevant to Oxystorm (my reading). summary.Summary: Morgan Griffiths of Lumina Intelligence argued that GLP-1, bad news for food and drink brands, is an opportunity for active nutrition [00:08]. He said 6.1% of the UK population currently take GLP-1s, 5.7% have taken them and 15.1% are considering them, about 18.4 million people, with similar current use in Italy, France, Germany and Spain [00:08]. Current users are mostly female, Gen X or Millennial and ABC1, already health-minded and willing to pay more; two thirds expect to spend the same or more on food and drink, and near 60% are likely to increase their supplement use [00:08]. He pointed to three opportunity areas: side effects, nutrition gaps such as protein and muscle loss, and lapsed users, who he said are four times more likely to regain weight according to a British Medical Association study [00:08]. Huel, Cambridge Nutrition, Portion IQ and Boots are already moving, and Lumina forecasts UK current use at around 11% by 2031 [00:08].
summary.Key takeaways:
- UK use now: 6.1% currently taking GLP-1s, 5.7% previously, 15.1% considering; he said the considering figure jumped "by about two thirds, a third to a half" when the pill was introduced [00:08].
- Together that is about 18.4 million people: everyone in the UK born since 2000, the UK's Netflix subscribers, or the 12th largest country in Europe [00:08].
- A summer study found similar current use in Italy, France, Germany and Spain; the US is further ahead [00:08].
- Current users (6.1%) outnumber vegans and vegetarians combined (5.7%), yet food and drink teams invest more in vegan innovation [00:08].
- Current users are not the obesity population the drugs were designed for: 56% female, 63% Gen X or Millennial, 63% ABC1 [00:08].
- They are health-minded: over 55% already make healthy lifestyle choices, 62% look for food with added benefits and 74% are happy to pay more for quality [00:08].
- Spend: the most common answer was no change, the net was an increase, and two thirds expect to spend the same or more on food and drink; 90 to 95% in the UK buy the drugs privately, at "one to 300 pounds a month" [00:08].
- Supplements: near 60% are likely to increase supplement use, near 90% with no change included; the list held no surprises, with creatine "maybe slightly higher" than expected, and he saw "a little bit of white space" for active nutrition [00:08].
- Opportunity areas: lapsed users (30% worry about putting weight back on), side effects, reduced food enjoyment and access to nutrition (muscle loss concerns, difficulty consuming enough protein and nutrients), with a malnutrition risk for people who eat less without care [00:08].
- Lapsed users: around 80% think they will keep the weight off (95% including neutral), but he cited a British Medical Association study showing people are four times more likely to regain weight lost with GLP-1 than with traditional methods [00:08].
- Why: GLP-1 changes behaviour without the user changing behaviour; when "you turn the tap off", the weight comes back unless habits changed [00:08].
- Market moves: Huel's lighter version, Cambridge Nutrition and Portion IQ ranges, and Boots' GLP-1 bays and shelf clips; putting GLP-1 on pack is "a kind of a health claim", so retailer support matters [00:08].
- Forecast: Lumina's data has UK current users growing to around 11% by 2031 [00:08].
- The talk's own recording starts at 16:05 and ends at about 16:24; the next recording (from-hype-to-proof-the-science) starts 12 seconds later, so the two do not overlap (my reading of the recording times).
summary.For Vita Actives: GLP-1 users are affluent, health-minded and expect to spend more on supplements, and protein and muscle loss are among their stated concerns [00:08]. My reading is that this is a direct opening for IsoClr: Pea in low-volume, high-protein products, and for CreaWin, since creatine already shows up higher than expected in what users take [00:08]. Lapsed users are his largest gap; my reading is that muscle-retention products (protein plus creatine) for people coming off the drugs are a concept to put to customers. The claims point matters: brands avoid "GLP-1" on pack and rely on retailer bays like Boots', so supplier support should be evidence on muscle and protein, not GLP-1 wording [00:08] (my reading). The survey covers the UK and four big EU markets, which matches our customers' markets [00:08]. Relevance high: GLP-1 nutrition and market structure.

summary.Summary: Gulrez Zariwala, founder director of the Centre for Nutraceuticals, reviewed what science supports supplements aimed at GLP-1 and satiety [00:15]. He explained that gut hormones (GLP-1 and PYY) signal fullness and ghrelin hunger, and that GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%" but can cost muscle as well as fat [00:15]. Of the supplement candidates, he said proteins have "an undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion, while berberine, cinnamon and bitter compounds have modest effects and few human studies [00:15]. His centre's own trial found potato protein and whey protein isolate raised GLP-1 equally, and a new trial of a mulberry extract (Otter: "Redicools") found significant rises in GLP-1 and falls in appetite and "food noise" [00:15]. He closed by saying no natural supplement can match a drug's effect, so expectations need managing and products need scientific validation [00:15].
summary.Key takeaways:
- The Centre for Nutraceuticals, in central London, aims to bridge industry and academia with independent research, from formulation and cell studies to human trials, sponsored or blue-sky [00:15].
- Obesity: incidence is high at 40% in the US and 35 to 40% in parts of South America and Africa; BMI over 30 is the simple consensus definition [00:15].
- Drug history: most obesity drugs were withdrawn; centrally acting ones such as rimonabant ("rimonaban" in Otter) carried neuropsychiatric risks, which turned the field to gut hormones [00:15].
- Gut hormones: ghrelin signals hunger; GLP-1, PYY, oxyntomodulin and GIP signal fullness; he said PYY is the more potent anorexigenic hormone, but GLP-1 drugs came first for commercial and clinical reasons [00:15].
- GLP-1 drugs give weight loss of "between five to 15%"; side effects include nausea and vomiting, loss of facial fat pads, collagen breakdown, and loss of body weight rather than body fat, so muscle loss "can lead to sarcopenia" [00:15].
- GLP-1 is not banned in sport but is "on the watch list", and he said athletes have noticed reduced inflammation and more energy [00:15].
- The supplement boom (Expo West, last year) brought "some high-profile lawsuits", regulatory clampdowns and lower consumer confidence [00:15].
- Proteins: an "undisputed effect" on GLP-1 secretion, depending on quality and amino acid profile; a 2015 study of high protein against high carbohydrate and high fat showed a significant post-meal rise in GLP-1 and PYY [00:15].
- Other candidates: OEA acts directly (GPR119) but degrades fast, so formulation may help; berberine's GLP-1 effects are indirect, mostly in rodents, and modest; cinnamon and bitter compounds have mechanisms but "mild to modest" effects and few human studies [00:15].
- His protein appetite trial (placebo-controlled triple crossover, isocaloric breakfasts): potato protein and whey protein isolate both raised GLP-1 significantly and equally; whey protein isolate also raised GIP significantly at 60 minutes, which he called the first nutraceutical showing a similar trend to the dual drugs, "not to the same magnitude" [00:15].
- The mulberry extract trial (with a UK company Otter heard as "Finova"; triple crossover with placebo, the extract, and a leading US GLP-1 brand's combination): a significant rise in GLP-1 at 180 minutes, a significant fall in appetite, and a significant fall in food noise over 24 hours ("19 with one and 21 with the other"); it finished last month, will be submitted next week, and follow-on studies are planned for 2027-28 if the partner supports them [00:15].
- Conclusions: supplements "may fill a gap" for current or lapsed users, but "There is no natural supplement solution that can match the magnitude of response" of a drug; validated products "increase market resilience"; GLP-1 use creates secondary demand for probiotics, proteins, fibre and multivitamins [00:15].
summary.For Vita Actives: A plant protein matched whey protein isolate on GLP-1 response in his trial; that was potato protein, not pea [00:15]. My reading is that this opens a satiety angle for IsoClr: Pea, but only with our own data, and his centre runs exactly this protocol for industry partners. Muscle loss on GLP-1 drugs is his headline risk, and protein is the one supplement class he called validated on both satiety and muscle [00:15]; my reading is that protein for GLP-1 users is a pitch with science behind it, while CreaWin's place there would rest on its muscle evidence, which he did not discuss. His warning on overclaiming (lawsuits, clampdowns) fits EU claims rules: we should not let customers imply GLP-1 effects for our ingredients [00:15] (my reading). items.title: Nick Morgan: how longevity is sold, from hallmarks to habits
items.to_check: The recording holds only the last six minutes of the talk, so the billed title, the speaker's organisation and role (Nutrition Integrated is not said in the recording), the five points he refers back to, and the room are unconfirmed.

summary.Summary: The recording catches the last six minutes of Nick Morgan's talk on the longevity consumer. He argued that longevity now sits inside women's health, menopause and sports nutrition, and that consumers connect with "energy and vitality" and "cellular health" rather than the hallmarks of ageing: of about 300 products coded, 9% refer to the hallmarks and, he thinks, only 4% put them in lead copy [00:00]. Brands sell routines, not single products; Solero's AM, PM and two-days-a-month reset was his example [00:00]. Longevity is one of the most expensive categories per serve, and an existing ingredient such as creatine, at a median of around 50 cents a serve, can be made premium by putting longevity on the front [00:00]. Formats are moving beyond capsules (70% of products) into liquids, chocolate, gummies, an NAD energy drink and a spermidine pen, and longevity is moving into hydration and sports nutrition, with Sergio Ramos's brand Centenarian as the example [00:00].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Consumers buy "energy and vitality" and "cellular health"; the hallmarks of ageing are "for this people in this room" [00:00].
- Of about 300 products coded, 9% refer to the hallmarks and only 4%, he thinks, put them in lead copy [00:00].
- "You don't sell one product in 2026": brands sell a routine of about three products, and an ingredient is sold on how it fits the customer's product system [00:00].
- Longevity products are among the most expensive per serve; the creatine median is about 50 cents a serve, and the same ingredient labelled longevity can be "a hell of a lot more expensive" [00:00].
- 70% of longevity products are capsules, but liquids, chocolate, gummies, drinks and injection pens are arriving [00:00].
- Cellular claims are entering hydration, and longevity is shifting into sports nutrition (Centenarian, linked to Sergio Ramos) [00:00].
- Among the ingredients on the longevity shelf he named resveratrol, CoQ10, ubiquinol and spermidine [00:00].
summary.For Vita Actives: The clearest point for us is the price gap: creatine at about 50 cents a serve against longevity products that are far more expensive [00:00]. My reading: a CreaWin pitch to brands building a longevity or healthy-ageing line, priced above the sports shelf, is open, and the speaker calls creatine "a daily essential" for himself. His shift of longevity into sports nutrition and hydration is the direction our customers are already travelling, so an AM/PM routine from a sports brand may carry creatine and protein as its daily pillars (my reading). summary.Summary: Miguel (business development) and Brian Keogh (chief scientific officer) of Nuritas, Dublin, presented the company's own AI platform for finding bioactive peptides and the evidence for PeptiStrong, a fava bean protein hydrolysate. PeptiStrong is said to target the mTOR pathway to build muscle and the NF kappa B pathway to lower inflammation; in a murine hind-limb unloading model it prevented 50% of the muscle loss [03:56]. Three human trials were shown: an immobilisation study in the Netherlands against a milk protein concentrate control, where strength came back to baseline and muscle protein synthesis was higher; a 14-day study in a Dublin sports clinic where strength went above baseline within two and a half weeks of a damaging exercise bout; and a KGK trial in Canada in untrained men and women, with faster strength gains at day 28 and 56, lower GDF15 and more bone mineral content [03:56]. Nuritas says PeptiStrong boosts protein rather than competing with it, and could add to creatine, leucine and HMB [03:56]. summary.Summary: Oliver of Kaneka presented ubiquinol, the reduced and active form of coenzyme Q10, which Kaneka makes in Japan. He argued that from about 30 the enzyme diaphorase falls away, so the body converts less Q10 to ubiquinol and should be given the active form directly [00:00]. He cited a blood test in which 90 mg of ubiquinol gave the same blood level as 300 mg of Q10, and said Q10 above 300 mg a day is not converted [00:00]. Kaneka recommends 100 mg a day, up to 300 mg for people on statins, under stress or seeking to have children, and lists heart, energy, mitochondrial, reproductive, cognition and menopause benefits, resting on what he said are more than 100 studies [00:00]. The ingredient comes pure for softgels, gel pills and gummies or microencapsulated for other formats, with halal certification, a partnership with Borussia Dortmund's women's team and a warehouse in Belgium for short lead times [00:00].

- Ubiquinol is the active form of CoQ10; the speaker says the converting enzyme diaphorase is no longer available as you get older, from about 30 [00:00].

summary.Summary: Two short talks in one recording. Each formulation is unique to its ingredient; ready products include NovaSol curcumin, astaxanthin and coenzyme Q10, for capsules, shots and combinations [00:18]. Balchem's Lena Leder, senior manager nutrition science, then began on OptiMSM: Balchem has 33 active research projects across chelated minerals, choline, vitamin K2 and methylfolate [09:04], and MSM is 34% sulfur by weight with evidence, she said, for joint and skin health and exercise recovery [10:40]. The recording ends about three minutes into her talk, before the data.

items.to_check: Billed title, Ralph's surname and role, the exact name of the new unit (he said "Martin Bauer Nutritions"; Otter heard "Nathan Bawa Nutraceuticals"), the room, and the spellings of the marker compounds and the Polish sites are unconfirmed.

summary.Summary: Ralph of Martin Bauer Nutraceuticals, a new unit of the family-owned Nature Network (Martin Bauer, Finzelberg, PhytoLab; 4,300 people, over 30 sites, several in Poland), introduced Rhosera, an extract of cultivated Rhodiola rosea aimed at the ageing muscle. His case: by 2050 probably over 2 billion people will be 60 or older; with age the muscle cell uses protein less efficiently (anabolic resistance), which is why protein advice rises from 0.8 to 1.2 g, and hardly any ingredient addresses that gap [00:00]. Wild rhodiola is overharvested, adulterated and, he said, listed as endangered in 2023, so Martin Bauer has cultivated it for 25 years: over 240 accessions reduced over ten years to three elite lines, grown under controlled integrated cultivation in Central Europe, with the root taking three to four years [00:00]. The cultivated material has four to five times the precursor compounds of wild material and, in muscle cells, switches on Pax7, MyoD and polyamine pathways that wild material does not unless concentrated 2.5-fold [00:00]. A double-blind, placebo-controlled trial in 140 untrained adults aged 55 to 75, all training and all given protein, with 400 mg of Rhosera each morning, reduced delayed-onset muscle soreness by 46% in men and 52% in women against 18% and 11% on placebo, and improved chair stand, single-leg balance, bench press, leg press, fatigue and quality of life, "statistically highly significant" by his account [00:00]. Preclinical work is published in Antioxidants and the human paper is in progress; he recommends 250 to 350 mg, and because rhodiola has no EFSA claim, brands borrow magnesium or vitamin B fatigue claims [00:00].

summary.Summary: Marit Weinstra of HMT, a branding and innovation agency for food and supplements, opened the probiotic programme by arguing that the biotics market (probiotics, prebiotics, fibres, postbiotics) has grown into "a jungle of products" and that consumers say they do not feel informed about probiotics [00:24]. She traced four eras: Yakult's daily ritual and the idea of good bacteria; Danone Activia making digestion benefits tangible, which led to competition on CFU count; a survival era where technology became the story; and the current shift from adding bacteria to nourishing the gut ecosystem, with the gut as the gateway to the rest of the body [00:24] [03:59]. From that she gave four rules for winning today: quality and proof over "more is better", feeding the whole ecosystem, measurable and felt benefits, and everyday food formats [03:59]. Her evidence was market examples: a US brand built on an Akkermansia strain for metabolic health, fibre brands selling plant diversity, brands setting expectations by week and month, and Poppi as a format consumers like [03:59]. Because most of these claims cannot be made in Europe, she said the brand has to carry them: a "double IP" of rational science plus an emotional brand [03:59].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Consumers say they do not feel informed about probiotics; the category has too many options and not enough clarity [00:24].
- The category was born as a daily ritual in a convenient format (Yakult), then competed on CFU count (after Activia made digestion tangible), then on survival and technology, and now on nourishing the gut ecosystem [00:24] [03:59].
- Rule 1: 50, 80 or 100 billion CFU on shelf means nothing to the consumer; numbers alone no longer build trust, so be the proven expert in a niche, as a US Akkermansia brand does for metabolic health and weight management [03:59].
- Rule 2: talk about feeding what the consumer already has, fibres and plant diversity, which they can see and act on; fibre brands lead this language [03:59].
- Rule 3: early adopters measure with microbiome tests and apps; mass-market consumers keep buying only when they feel a difference, so brands now set expectations for one week and one month [03:59].
- Rule 4: consumers stick with formats they like; Poppi is her example of a product designed around the consumer rather than the ingredient [03:59].
- In Europe most of these claims cannot be made, so the brand must carry them: brand the strain and build a "double IP", rational and emotional [03:59].
- The chair placed HMT as helping companies connect what they can develop with what consumers understand and value [00:00].

My reading: "science opens the doors, but it's a brand that keeps you in the room" is an argument for branded ingredients with a story a European brand can tell within claim rules. summary.Summary: Ariel Annoni, who runs Novonesis's human health business across Central and Eastern Europe, the Middle East and Africa, argued that a successful probiotic product needs the right science, quality, manufacturing partner and brand strategy, not just a good ingredient [00:42]. She introduced Novonesis as the combination of Novozymes and Chr. Hansen with more than 100 years of expertise, a portfolio of probiotics, postbiotics, enzymes, vitamins and HMOs, and strains (Otter heard "GGM BB 12") that she called among the most documented in the world [00:42]. She said the European probiotic market is growing in digestive, immune and women's health and healthy ageing, and named four trends: more specialised needs, professional-recommended probiotics, applications beyond gut health, and growth from digital channels and emerging markets [00:42]. Alessia of Montefarmaco, an Italian family pharmaceutical company founded in 1945, told the Lactoflorene story: a partnership with Novonesis since the early 2000s that began with an Italian requirement for at least 1 billion CFU in a volume-limited cap, a core formula unchanged for almost 20 years, a clinical study on the finished product, and today third place in Italy with a share of around 7% [09:06]. The chair closed by saying both morning talks came back to the consumer asking "what's in it for me" [14:17].

- Novonesis pitches to CMOs and CDMOs directly: probiotic solutions "already supported by research, market experience, and technical know-how", with the aim of a product the consumer will trust and repurchase, not only an ingredient sale [00:42].
- Science is strain specific; some strains have limited documentation, others decades of study, and documented strains protect the reputation of the brand the manufacturer makes [00:42].
- Growth areas named: digestive health, immune health, women's health, healthy ageing; new categories cardiovascular and mental health [00:42].

items.title: Sacco System: probiotic CDMO services, CA15 for women's health and Symbio for healthy ageing
items.to_check: The speaker never gives his name on the recording (which starts mid-introduction): "Simone" comes from the Nordic Biotic speaker's reference to "Simone from Saco" in the next talk and the chair thanks him with a word Otter heard as "Salami", so name, surname and role are unconfirmed, as are the billed title, the room, and the opening minutes missed by the recording; times are the recording's, Pacific converted to Polish time.

summary.Summary: The recording joins Sacco System's speaker mid-introduction. He presented Sacco as a family company founded in 1872, selling in more than 110 countries, with plants in Como and Milan (the sister company CSL, pharmaceutical API probiotics), a plant in Wisconsin and a pilot for next-generation bacteria in Brisbane [00:00]. He described GMP pharma and GMP food-grade sites, strains screened to EFSA requirements across more than 30 species, a "made-for-you" service developing strains for third parties, and a recent investment in clinical studies and patents in two areas, women's health and healthy ageing [00:00]. CA15, a patented strain isolated from healthy women in 2022, was tested by the University of Catania in an exploratory study of six women and a study of 200 women with bacterial vaginosis and vulvovaginal candidiasis, 10 days of oral intake and a one-month washout; he reported less burning, discomfort, itching, secretions and inflammation and, one month after stopping, 98% with a restored pH range and 92% with a negative amine test [00:00]. Symbio, a 1:1 mix of paracasei and rhamnosus strains isolated from centenarians in the Marche region, was tested in a randomised, double-blind, placebo-controlled study of 97 elderly subjects over six months; he reported more lactobacilli, bifidobacteria and butyrate, a 43% reduction in high-sensitivity C-reactive protein, an improvement in IGF-1, which he linked to protein synthesis and muscle mass, and a slower reduction in telomere length [00:00].

- Sacco System: family company since 1872, more than 110 countries, plants in Como, Milan (CSL, pharma API probiotics) and Wisconsin, a Brisbane pilot for next-generation and exotic strains [00:00].

- Offer: probiotics, postbiotics and customised mixtures; "culture science" strains with clinical studies and "culture select" strains screened to EFSA requirements, more than 30 species; strain development for third parties [00:00].

- He said the strain survives the gut, reaches the vagina and promotes the natural lactobacilli while reducing enterococci and Gardnerella vaginalis [00:00].

items.title: SPI Pharma and Nordic Biotic: new dosage forms and clinically tested strains
ingredients: Composol Pro Tab (SPI Pharma, as heard; polyol-based chewable platform)
GLP-1 companion product (Nordic Biotic and Azento)
items.to_check: Billed titles of the two talks, the SPI Pharma speaker's full name (the chair calls him Miguel; the recording starts mid-talk, a 22-second Otter fragment at 11:02 holds his opening words), the Nordic Biotic speaker's name spelling (Otter: Mihail Jakubowski; the chair said "Mikhail"; he said something Otter heard as "Mihaj Kuboski"), both roles, the exact spelling of the SPI platform heard as "composol pro tab", and the room are unconfirmed; times are the recording's, Pacific converted to Polish time.

summary.Summary: The recording joins Miguel of SPI Pharma mid-talk. He showed three dosage-form concepts: chewable probiotic tablets on a polyol-based, low-water-activity platform (heard as "composol pro tab") compressed at low force so the probiotics survive, with a live product shown under Favea's branding [00:01]; effervescent hydration formats (tablets, stick packs, sachets) stabilised with Effer Soda, a sodium bicarbonate partly transformed to carbonate to form a protective layer, which can also give a "delicate fizz" in chewables and fast melts that distracts the tongue from bitterness [00:01]; and fast-melt (orally disintegrating) tablets for children, elderly people with dysphagia and anyone who dislikes swallowing [00:01]. His close, aimed at the capsule maker ACG: "don't ask your consumer to swallow another capsule" [07:50]. Mihail Jakubowski of Nordic Biotic (a silver sponsor) said the company supplies clinically tested probiotics to brand owners, CDMOs and distributors with full exclusivity by territory at the strain level, and works from genomics to metabolomics (630 molecules measured), functional testing and human studies [09:25]. He presented Northbiotic Mental Balance (Lactobacillus plantarum 140 producing GABA and Bifidobacterium breve 010 producing a B vitamin), tested for eight weeks in 227 students at exam time, 219 completing, with results received the week before; he said statistical efficacy was proved for sleep quality and stress [09:25]. He also showed a microplastic blend of Lactobacillus acidophilus 120 (binds) and Lactobacillus fermentum 160 (pushes away), with a human study in progress and an invitation to a "plastic gut-free initiative" [09:25].
summary.Key takeaways:
- Chewable probiotic tablets: a polyol-based platform with low water content and water activity, compressed at low force, sweet without sugar; probiotics survive the process; shown in a real Favea product [00:01].
- Hydration is a trend in supplements and beverages; effervescence relies on sodium bicarbonate, which with an acid is hygroscopic and unstable over shelf life; Effer Soda is SPI Pharma's stabilised form for tablets, stick packs and sachets [00:01].
- A delicate fizz in chewables or fast melts is also a way to distract the tongue from bitterness [00:01].
- Fast-melt tablets need no water and suit children, elderly people with dysphagia and people who dislike swallowing; SPI Pharma offers an ODT platform that can carry fizz [00:01].
- SPI Pharma's role, as he put it, is creating product concepts so a CDMO can expand into new dosage forms; "we do not limit there" [00:01].
- Nordic Biotic: full exclusivity by territory at strain level; genomics, then metabolomics (630 molecules, "the postbiotics actually"), then functional testing, then human studies; CFU measured to milligrams [09:25].
- Mental Balance: strains chosen for what they produce (L. plantarum 140, GABA; B. breve 010, a B vitamin); eight-week study, 227 students started, 219 completed, "one of the largest study in stress in probiotics in the last decade"; results received last week; he said statistical efficacy was proved in sleep quality and stress [09:25].
- Microplastic blend: L. acidophilus 120 aggregates microplastic, L. fermentum 160 pushes it away; offered as a standalone or an add-on to a gut, detox or clean-label formula; the human study is in progress [09:25].
- Nordic Biotic has a GLP-1 companion product with its Swiss sister company Azento; gut-skin, gut-bone and gut-brain technologies were named [09:25].
- WIPO innovation index as he cited it: of 12 countries, seven are European; in the region Latvia, Czechia, Hungary and Poland lead [09:25].
- The chair's aside: Coca-Cola was first sold as a medicinal tonic for brain and nerves [08:30].
summary.For Vita Actives: Medium relevance, the highest of the four: formats, not ingredients. Hydration sticks, effervescent tablets, chewables and fast melts are the formats our sports and active nutrition customers sell, and SPI Pharma's platforms are what a CDMO uses to make them. My reading: a CreaWin chewable or fast-melt tablet, and creatine or electrolytes in a stable effervescent stick, are format questions to raise with the CDMOs who work with SPI Pharma and Favea; Favea (shown making a live product) is a CDMO to know. My reading: Nordic Biotic's GLP-1 companion product is the adjacent opportunity for IsoClr: Pea, since protein for muscle preservation on GLP-1 drugs is a brief our customers already have; its stress and sleep blend sits next to recovery positioning in active nutrition. Nordic Biotic's exclusivity-by-territory model is a pattern a branded ingredient supplier can study (my reading). All efficacy claims are the speakers' and the Mental Balance study is unpublished as of the talk.
